Hi Zoharlyn,

The paper where this method is derived is here:

https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.13270

The reason discussed there (with some references) is that the method (perturbatively) has the same order of bias as REML, which varies from second order to none, depending on the model structure.

Very large area estimates resulting from very large range crossing timescales is one way that you could classify non-residents.

Best,
Chris

Hello Chris,

Happy New Year! After a recent conversation with my committee, it was decided that we are actually going to implement the iRSF approach available in the ctmm package! I'm still going to compare habitat variables in the core use and home range contours, but through non-RSF techniques such as regression or comparisons of means.

I also have a conceptual question: considering that the domain of availability with these iRSFs is a Gaussian area around the home range rather than entirely within the home range itself, is this still considered third order selection? Or something else entirely?

Thanks for the help!

Best,
Tyler

For regularizing the data, you could use predict() or simulate(), depending on what you want to do with that.
